And in his rage he took captives from Mesopotamia and left.
And when Constantine went out to wage war with the Persians and reached Nicomedia, he fell ill,
and he died there.
And he made a will,
and entrusted the kingdom to his three sons.
And he delivered the will into the hands of a certain priest, an Arian.
And when he died, his body was conveyed to Constantinople,
having lived twenty-four years {OCR?: his sons/the years of his reign?}.
Constantine the Victorious had three sons:
the eldest, Constantine, named after his father;
the middle one, Constantis (Constantius?);
and the youngest, Custus (Constans?).
While during his lifetime he had appointed the eldest as Caesar in Constantinople,
and the middle one in Antioch and all (Mesopotamia and the eastern) the East,
and the youngest in Rome.
And when the Victorious died,
that middle son,
as one who was close by,
came first.
And he made a covenant with that Arian priest,
that he would persecute everyone who said 'of the same essence' (consubstantial).
And he delivered the will to him,
and he brought his father in a golden coffin into the royal city.
Now when Shapur heard about the Victorious that he had died,
he went up again against Nisibis,
which is on the border between the Romans and the Persians,
and it was called Antioch of Mygdonia.
And he besieged it for seventy days,
and built siege mounds against it.
And he made a great dam against the flow of the river Mygdonius, which enters and divides its midst.
And when the water overflowed above the wall,
and it could not withstand the pressure,
it tottered and fell.
And when Shapur thought that without any toil he would capture it,
he saw another, new wall that had already been built.
And also the blessed Ephrem went up on the wall to curse the barbarians.
And he prayed to God,
and He brought upon them swarms of flies and gnats.
And the elephants especially were distressed,
because their skin was bare.
And they also entered the nostrils and ears of the horses,
and they snapped their bridles and threw their riders and fled.
And Shapur returned in shame.
